lesson.title: Blood & Kin
lesson.subtitle: Vater ↔ father (Verner's law, not V→B), Mutter, Sohn, Tochter — the family as cognate wall

hook.title: The Family Reunion Is a Cognate Wall
hook.content: The core kin words are almost all exact twins: Mutter/mother (essentially unchanged), Sohn/son (the h was once heard), Bruder/brother (th→d), Schwester/sister (sw→schw), Tochter/daughter (a double-shift showpiece: d→t AND gh→ch). One word wears a warning label: Vater/father is NOT the V→B family — the v in Vater is pronounced [f], and English f ↔ German v=[f] here is Verner's law, the ancient voicing rule that made 'father' and 'Vater' both keep their old f-sound while brothers like geben/give drifted to b. And the parents themselves are a grammar riddle: Eltern is literally 'the elder ones' — a frozen comparative of alt that became the whole word for parents.

footnotes.title: Verner's Law in One Breath
footnotes.content: Before the Germanic sound shifts, the f/th/h family voiced between vowels under Verner's law — which is why father/Vater both have their ancient fricative while brother/Bruder hardened to b. If V→B applied to Vater, German would say *Bater. It does not: the v IS the [f]. Trust the IPA, not the spelling.

pattern.title: Possession Runs on mein/meine
pattern.content: Mein Vater, meine Mutter, mein Sohn, meine Tochter — the possessor echoes the noun's gender (possessive ladders, sprig 1103, at work). Sentences: Mein Bruder lernt Deutsch. Meine Schwester ist Lehrerin. Meine Eltern wohnen in Hamburg (Eltern is plural-only — 'the elders', so meine, not mein). And the diminutive you will hear all day: die Mädchen (girl, neuter because -chen is always neuter) — das Mädchen, not die. Kin vocabulary is where German grammar and cognate memory meet: every family sentence rehearses both.
pattern.linguist_note: Tochter and daughter are the trail's double-shift trophy: Proto-Germanic *duhtēr → German hardened d→t and gh→ch; English kept both ancient sounds and spelled them daughter. Say both words aloud — you are hearing the same word twice, 1,500 years apart in drift.

exercises.prompt: Match the kin cognates. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:

matching_pairs.english: the whole family (every generation under one roof)

exercises.target_answer: der Vater, die Mutter, der Sohn, die Tochter, die Schwester, die Familie, Wir können Max heißen, Wir können buchstabieren, ein Buchstabe
exercises.meaning: father (Verner's law, NOT V→B); mother (essentially unchanged); son (the h was once heard); daughter (double shift: d→t + gh→ch); sister (sw→schw); the whole family (every generation under one roof); We can be called Max; We can spell; a letter of the alphabet
exercises.explanation: Five twins and one warning label: Vater's v is [f] — Verner's law, not the V→B shift that turned give into geben.

exercises.prompt: Tochter ↔ daughter carries TWO shifts: d→t and:
exercises.explanation: The silent gh in daughter was once sounded — German Nacht-style ch keeps it: Tochter. Same double shift as Nacht/night.
A frozen comparative of alt (old): elter- is elder. German says 'the elders' where English coined 'parents'.

exercises.prompt: Which English word is the twin of 'Sohn'?
exercises.explanation: The h in Sohn was once pronounced — *sunuh- — but the twinship is total: son and Sohn are one word.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the sentence: 'My parents live in Hamburg'
exercises.meaning: Meine Eltern wohnen in Hamburg = my parents live in Hamburg

vocab_hints.note: ich wohne in... — the residence verb

exercises.explanation: Eltern is plural, so it takes meine and the -en verb form — the elders, treated as the plural they are. And the moment you meet the rest of die Familie, you ask their names: Wie schreibt man das? — one Buchstabe at a time.

summary.outcome: Name the core family with correct possessives, and explain the Verner's-law trap in Vater.

use_example.german: Mein Vater ist alt, aber meine Mutter ist Lehrerin.
use_example.english: My father is old, but my mother is a teacher.

summary.takeaway: Mutter, Sohn, Bruder, Schwester, Tochter — all twins; Vater wears Verner's law; Eltern is 'the elder ones' frozen into a noun.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the extended clan — grandparents, in-laws and the compound principle that builds Großvater from parts you own.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "The father is here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Der Vater ist heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Blood & Kin.

vater.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fadēr; English f ↔ German v=[f] reflects Verner's-law voicing, not the v→b shift family. [wiktionary]

mutter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mōdēr — English mother and German Mutter are essentially unchanged siblings. [wiktionary]

sohn.context_phrase: Mein Sohn ist sechs Jahre alt.
sohn.context_translation: My son is six years old.
sohn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sunuz — the direct twin of English son (the historical h was once pronounced). [wiktionary]

schwester.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swestēr — sw- ↔ schw- beginning, otherwise essentially unchanged. [wiktionary]

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

bruder.etymology_derivation: Medial th shifted to d; unstressed -er vocalizes to [ɐ].

eltern.etymology_derivation: Plural-only; a nominalized comparative of alt (old) — literally 'the elder ones', kin to English old. [wiktionary]

familie.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin familia — the same Latin source as English family. [wiktionary]

buchstabe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, literally book-stave: each letter was a stave carved for writing, first on beechwood; the page compares English bookstaff and bookstave. [wiktionary]

tal.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch das Tal.
tal.context_translation: The river flows through the valley / dale.

tau.context_phrase: Morgens liegt Tau auf dem Gras.
tau.context_translation: In the morning dew lies on the grass.

fliege.context_translation: A fly buzzes in the room.

dachboden.context_phrase: Der Koffer ist auf dem Dachboden.
dachboden.context_translation: The suitcase is in the attic.
dachboden.etymology_derivation: Compound of Dach and Boden, literally roof floor; Dach corresponds to English thatch via the th to d shift, and Boden to English bottom via the d to t shift. [wiktionary]

heide.context_translation: The heath blooms in late summer.
heide.etymology_derivation: From Old High German heida, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþi, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī. English heath is the listed cognate, keeping the th where German has d. [wiktionary]

jeder.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ioweder (io 'ever' + wedar), the compound the page compares with English either; it originally meant each of two before merging with ieder. [wiktionary]

tauchen.context_translation: The diver dives in the sea.
tauchen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *dūkan (to dive) - the twin of English duck, shifted twice: d-to-t and k-to-ch, like day-Tag and make-machen. [wiktionary]

nachtisch.etymology_derivation: nach + Tisch, with Tisch in its archaic sense meal; the documented twin of dish (Latin discus, d to t), so a Nachtisch is literally an after-dish. [wiktionary]

raten.context_phrase: Ich rate dir zu einer Pause.
raten.context_translation: I advise you to take a break.
raten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *rēdaną — English read and archaic rede are documented cognates; German kept the advising sense and hardened d to t. [wiktionary]

hochhaus.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in einem alten Hochhaus.
hochhaus.context_translation: We live in an old high-rise.
hochhaus.etymology_derivation: hoch + Haus — the high house, what English calls a high-rise; hoch is the twin of high (gh → ch). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops. This gives you an instant key to dozens of core words.
th_to_d.literature_source: Documented in Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar as the primary dental hardening of the Second Sound Shift.
